recent_decisions.decision: The leaf tufts were geometrically cubes, and the gate that could see it had to be built before the fix could be judged.
recent_decisions.why: The operator said "the bunches of leaves look a little weird, kind of like they are cubes." The first instrument grouped cards by PROXIMITY and reported 0.31 against a 0.30 threshold - nearly a false pass. Grouping exactly (one emit_sleeve call is one sleeve) showed the truth: conifer tufts were 100% parallel card pairs, broadleaf tufts 67% perpendicular plus 33% parallel. The golden-angle azimuth fix alone left 33% still near-perpendicular because the normals stayed on one circle; the tilt half is what cleared it, and stratifying those tilts in solid-angle bands (right for POINTS) measured WORSE than no tilt at all, because a sleeve is a set of PLANES. Line packing, not point scattering.

recent_decisions.decision: The canopy parity gate records the level PER SPECIES rather than widening one band.
recent_decisions.why: Broadleaf crowns land on the isotropic leaf-angle kernel almost exactly (0.94-1.05). Fir and pine sit 22% under it at every sun angle, and that is real: a fir carries flat sprays along a branch and the spherify blend pushes its normals horizontal. A single band loose enough to admit 1.30 would stop noticing a broadleaf that broke. The ratio is near-constant in sun angle for every species, so the kernel SHAPE is right and only the LEVEL is species-dependent - driving those to 1.00 wants a per-species scalar baked into the billboard atlas, which is named as the follow-up rather than hidden.

recent_decisions.decision: The conifer card over-brightness was the odd component of the shading normals, not anisotropic foliage.
recent_decisions.why: I told the operator it was real fir anisotropy. Wrong. A crown area-weighted mean shading normal is nonzero (fir 0.1221 down to momiji 0.0217) and that ordering matches the brightness ordering exactly; it survives max(N.L,0) because a card gives both windings the same normal. Cancelled at source by solving for the correction that drives the mean to zero. An adversarial reviewer REFUTED the geometric just-so story offered for why the mean points down while reproducing the arithmetic, so the comments now say the first moment is measured, not derived. Recording a limitation in a gate was right while it was a limitation and wrong to keep once it was fixable.

recent_decisions.decision: A three-lane merge was committed under a one-lane message and immediately reset.
recent_decisions.why: git apply --3way STAGES what it applies. After applying three worktree patches, adding three files by name added to an index that already held all nine, so the commit swept every lane under a message describing one - the exact failure the shared-checkout rule exists to prevent. Caught by reading git show --stat AFTER committing, which is too late. Rule: after any git apply, run git reset before staging, and check git diff --cached --stat BEFORE the commit.

recent_decisions.decision: View-frustum culling of near trees is the largest verified unclaimed win: 62% of the draw budget is spent behind the camera.
recent_decisions.why: Measured at the operator settings two independent ways (engine harness plus first-principles geometry, agreeing within 1.5pp). Respending that budget on visible trees moves the model reach 181 m to 300 m, 2.9x the area for the same draw count. NOT a one-line change: three coverage rules were tested and only one works (visible trees feed ModelCoverage AND the hide radius is clamped by the harvest edge). Naive skip gives a 190 m bare ring in FRONT of the player; naive uncovered gives a 4.7 m radius so nothing ever hides. The cull bound must enclose the CARD (acacia is 1.365x height), not the trunk. The shadow pass must stay unculled: near-tree models are the only off-screen casters, and 44-61% of culled trees cast into view at an 8 degree sun. The v0.995 reason for view-independence died with the v0.1110.2 ModelCoverage rewrite.
